analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to residents who buy in, with income-capped premiums, higher federal matching funds, and required reproductive coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 22, 2024, drew 17 Democratic cosponsors, and received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let each state decide whether to open its Medicaid program to any resident who isn't already covered, letting them buy in like an insurance plan. Premiums could not exceed 8.5 percent of a family's income, and regular premium tax credits could be applied to lower the cost. It would also give holdout states the same higher federal Medicaid match that expansion states got, require state Medicaid programs to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care including abortion, and guarantee primary care doctors Medicare-level payment rates in Medicaid. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured residents in states that choose to participate, who would gain a low-cost public coverage option with premiums capped at 8.5 percent of household income and standard premium tax credits applied [S2][S3]. People in the ten or so states that never expanded Medicaid would benefit from the higher federal matching rate the bill extends regardless of when a state expands [S2][S3]. Medicaid enrollees would gain guaranteed coverage of comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion [S2][S3]. Primary care providers treating Medicaid patients would be paid at least Medicare rates, which supporters argued would widen the network of doctors willing to see them [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured residents in participating states

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a state-option Medicaid buy-in: any resident not already eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage could buy into the state Medicaid plan beginning January 1, 2025, at the option of the state [S2][S3].

Premiums for buy-in participants are capped at 8.5 percent of family household income, and other cost-sharing must follow Affordable Care Act limits; buy-in enrollees also qualify for the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions as Marketplace plan customers [S3].

The bill rewrites the enhanced federal Medicaid matching rate so every state that expands Medicaid gets the enhanced rate on the same schedule, regardless of when it expands, removing the financial penalty states that delayed expansion currently face [S2][S3].

State Medicaid programs would be required to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care services, including abortion services and abortion-related services, as a condition of plan approval [S2][S3].

The bill revives a Medicare payment rate floor for primary care services under Medicaid and extends it to nurse practitioners, physician assistants, certified nurse-midwives, and community clinics, and requires Medicaid managed care contracts to pay those providers at the required rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the 90 percent federal match on buy-in administrative costs, the extended enhanced matching rate for late-expanding states, and a $50 million appropriation for quality-measure updates [S3]. Private health insurers would lose potential customers in states that adopt the buy-in, since a cheaper public plan would compete with Marketplace and employer plans. States that opt in would shoulder any administrative burden not covered by the federal match.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and private health insurers

drawbacks.text: The buy-in is optional for states, so residents in states that decline to participate get nothing; the bill provides no mechanism to compel state adoption [S2][S3].

Premiums for buy-in participants can run up to 8.5 percent of family income, which is a real cost for moderate-income households even with tax credits, and cost-sharing reductions are subject to the existing income eligibility threshold [S3].

Medicaid historically pays doctors less than private insurance, and the bill addresses that only for primary care, not for specialties, so buy-in customers could still face narrow provider networks [S3].

The federal cost is open-ended: the enhanced matching rate for late-expanding states, the 90 percent administrative match, and the flow of premium tax credits through the program all add federal spending, and the bill's requirement that Medicaid cover abortion would trigger political and legal conflict in many states [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who cannot afford Marketplace premiums or fall into a coverage gap, a Medicaid buy-in with an 8.5 percent premium cap and standard tax credits would be a meaningful, well-designed option, and the Medicare-rate floor for primary care addresses the usual weakness of Medicaid networks. The main design tradeoffs are that participation is entirely at each state's option, the federal cost is open-ended, and the abortion-coverage mandate would sharply limit how many states would join. As written, its real-world reach depends entirely on how many states choose to participate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the State Public Option Act on March 22, 2024, with 16 other Democratic senators joining as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid [S5].
Seventeen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican senator did [S4].
No further action was ever recorded on the bill — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers are better off: no public plan competes with their Marketplace and employer-based coverage, and the existing insurance arrangements remain in place. So does the status quo for the states that have declined to expand Medicaid, which continue to face the existing matching-rate structure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the coverage status quo

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State Public Option Act and led its introduction with original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 22, 2024 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporting senators were Democrats (the sponsor plus 17 cosponsors of the 48-seat Democratic caucus), with no Republican support and no votes ever held, so the partisan shape is known only from sponsorship.

industries.note: In states that adopt the buy-in, a low-cost public plan would compete directly with private Marketplace and employer coverage, costing insurers customers. But Medicaid coverage is often delivered through private managed care contracts, and the bill explicitly allows buy-in enrollees to be enrolled in managed care, so many insurers could also end up administering the program they compete with.

industries.industry: Primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, and community health clinics
industries.note: The bill guarantees Medicaid payment of at least Medicare rates for primary care services and extends that floor to advanced-practice clinicians and clinics, raising revenue for the providers who treat low-income patients while improving access for enrollees.

Broader coverage through a buy-in would reduce uncompensated care costs hospitals currently absorb from uninsured patients, though the bill excludes emergency department services from the primary care rate floor.
